title: Short Link Service
statement:
Build a tiny link shortener with two calls:

  • shorten(longUrl) returns a short link for longUrl.
  • expand(shortUrl) returns the long URL that shortUrl was issued for, or "" if this service never issued that exact link.

Real shorteners may pick codes however they like. So that tests can check the output, our version fixes the scheme: the k-th distinct long URL ever shortened (counting from 1) gets "https://sho.rt/" + code, where code is k written in base 62 with the digits 0–9, then a–z, then A–Z. So the 1st URL gets /1, the 10th /a, the 36th /A and the 62nd /10. Shortening a URL that was already shortened returns its existing link and does not use up a number.

Both calls must run in time proportional to the URL length, not to the number of links issued. Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the service. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: The repeated URL gets its old link back, so only two numbers are used and /3 was never issued.
Before anything is shortened, nothing expands. "/01" is a different string from the issued "/1", so it is unknown too.

constraints: shortUrl can be any string up to 100 characters
hints: Two lookups are needed: from a long URL to its link (to reuse it) and from a link back to the URL. What gives both in O(1)?
Two hash maps, plus a counter for the next number to hand out.
To write k in base 62, repeatedly take k % 62 as the last digit and divide k by 62, building the code from the right.

explain.intuition:
A shortener is two lookup tables. One maps each long URL to its link, so a repeated request returns the same link instead of burning a new number. The other maps each issued link back to its long URL for expand. Both are hash maps, so each call is O(1) apart from reading the URL itself.

The codes come from a counter. Writing the counter in base 62 keeps links short: six characters already cover more than 56 billion URLs. That is the same idea real shorteners use, often with a random or shuffled alphabet so links are not guessable in order.
steps: Keep toShort and toLong maps and a counter next = 1.
shorten(url): if toShort has it, return the stored link.
Otherwise build the base-62 code of next, increment next, store the link in both maps and return it.
expand(link): return toLong.get(link), or "" if it is missing.
pitfalls: Issuing a new number for a URL that was already shortened. The scheme says the old link comes back.
Building the base-62 digits left to right. The remainder gives the last digit, so prepend each one.
Parsing any string that starts with the prefix as a number. "/01" would decode to 1, but it is not a link the service issued; a map lookup on the full string avoids that.

complexity.time: O(L) per call, L = URL length

solutions.title: List of issued links, searched linearly
solutions.idea: Keep the long URLs in a list in issue order. shorten searches the list for the URL; expand searches the issued links. Simple, but each call is O(number of links).

solutions.title: Two hash maps and a base-62 counter
solutions.idea: One map from long URL to link for reuse, one from link to long URL for expand. A counter written in base 62 makes each new code.

followups: Sequential codes let anyone enumerate every link. How would you make codes unguessable while keeping them short and collision-free?
The service runs on many servers at once. How do they hand out numbers without issuing the same one twice?
